claims.text: The as-synthesized equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles have a random atomic distribution.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down above approximately 600 K in sub-10 nm Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles.
Surface-energy-driven Ostwald ripening and kinetic segregation override thermodynamic stabilization above the breakdown temperature.
Surface diffusion and vapor-phase transport enable Ostwald ripening during vacuum heating.
During Ostwald ripening, smaller particles lose material that redeposits on larger particles.
Au and Pt are the low-surface-energy elements in this alloy.
Au and Pt migrate preferentially to nanoparticle surfaces during heating.
Surface segregation lowers surface energy while destabilizing the equiatomic solid solution.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of sub-10 nm particles amplifies surface effects and causes surface-controlled evolution to dominate.
Heating will cause the loss of particles smaller than 5 nm.
Heating will produce growth of larger particles to sizes above 10 nm.
The particles will evolve toward faceted or spherical morphologies as surface energy is minimized.
After heating, particle surfaces will be enriched in Au and Pt and depleted in Co, Cu, and Ni.
A high-configurational-entropy and sluggish-diffusion baseline predicts retention of equiatomic composition and particle size to higher temperatures.
The proposed surface-controlled breakdown regime applies to particles smaller than 10 nm.
For particles larger than 50 nm, bulk diffusion and sluggish kinetics may dominate.
The exact breakdown temperature and segregation kinetics depend on synthesis method and initial defect structure.
The relative contributions of surface diffusion and vapor transport vary with particle size and vacuum quality.
In-situ TEM heating with particle-size and composition monitoring can discriminate stable equiatomic particles from coarsening accompanied by Au/Pt surface segregation.
